newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian far right exploits split over bank sale.
newsitem.headline: Austrian far right exploits split over bank sale.

text.p: Far-right leader Joerg Haider, exploiting a split in Austria's government, said on Thursday his party was holding talks with conservatives in the ruling coalition over the planned privatisation of the country's second biggest bank.
Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's plan for the sale of Creditanstalt-Bankverein has driven a wedge between his Social Democrats and their conservative allies, the People's Party.
Creditanstalt was once the bankers of the Habsburg imperial family and is still considered a conservative fiefdom.
The People's Party fiercely objects to the prospect of it being taken over by rival Bank Austria, which is indirectly controlled by the Social Democrat-dominated City of Vienna.

Rightwinger Haider, who has made strong electoral gains in recent years but is frozen out of power by a socialist-conservative alliance, told a news conference: "We have already had several rounds of talks with (People's Party Economic Minister Johann) Farnleitner and his experts."
He said the two parties had found common ground on a number of points regarding the sale of the flagship bank but declined to give details.
The People's Party led by Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel has called for an emergency session of parliament next Tuesday. It could turn into a showdown between the two governing parties.

The conservatives, who could muster a majority in parliament if supported by Haider's far-right Freedom Party, would like to see Creditanstalt sold to an international consortium led by Italian-controlled insurer EA-Generali.
Chancellor Vranitzky has called a special session of coalition leaders on Monday in an attempt to defuse the crisis in his the one-year-old government.
Social Democrat Finance Minister Viktor Klima, who has sole responsibility for choosing the Creditanstalt buyer, said he hoped the conservatives would not force a government breakdown.
"That would mean fresh elections and the only one to profit from it would be Haider," he said in an interview in Thursday's edition of current affairs magazine News.

Haider's party scored nearly 28 percent in European elections last October, just a few thousand votes behind the two big parties which have ruled Austria alone or together since the end of World War Two.
Haider told reporters he did not believe the government would crumble over the Creditanstalt debacle.

The 47-year-old populist, who opposes the Maastricht treaty on closer European economic and political union, supports the Bank Austria bid for Creditanstalt as the "Austrian solution" but has put forward his own conditions to the sale, focusing on reform of the country's banking industry.
The final deadline for offers to buy Creditanstalt expires on Friday but the conservatives have cautioned Klima to wait until after parliament meets before making his decision.
Creditanstalt on Thursday reported what may be its last set of preliminary profit figures before the sale.

Group net earnings increased to 2.6 billion schillings ($235 million) in 1996 from 2.16 billion schillings ($196 million) a year earlier, helped by a nine-percent decline in risk provisions to about 3.1 billion schillings ($280 million).
